item.label: continuity_geometry_of_the_action_line
item.description: A single geometric construction generates most of this chapter's rules. Attention between subjects creates a sight line; tracing that sight line fixes the action line; the action line cuts the circle of possible camera positions into two halves; staying in one half preserves screen direction; crossing it reverses direction; and reciprocal coverage positions are computed by mirroring across the same line. The rules are consequences of one plan drawing, not a list.

whole_system_claim.text: Screen direction, the 180 degree rule, jumping the line, the 30 degree rule and reciprocating imagery are all derived from a single imaginary line established by the talent's own sight line. Once that line is fixed, the permitted camera positions, the mirrored positions for matched coverage and the failure mode of crossing it all follow geometrically.

source_ref.section: The Imaginary Line—The 180 Degree Rule; The 30 Degree Rule

dependencies.nature: the line is established by tracing a sight line
the arc is defined by the line
the 30 degree increments are measured within the arc

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: The derivation chain is the source's own: it states that the line is traced from the sight line, that the arc follows from the line, that the 30 degree slices sit within the arc, and that reciprocal setups mirror across it. What is ours is treating maintained screen direction as a property the system preserves rather than as a further member.

source_terms: A two-shot will establish frame left and frame right, therefore also establishing screen direction, look room, and lines of attention for the two characters.
Clearly, with both persons looking right, they would appear to be talking to some third, but unseen, person off-screen.
item.claim: The action line exists for people as well as movement. A two-shot fixes which character is frame left and which frame right, and with that the screen direction, the look room and each character's line of attention. Every coverage single must keep the characters on their established sides looking in their established directions. If one single is shot from the far side of the line, both characters appear to look the same way, so they read as addressing an unseen third person — which makes no sense to an audience who can account for only two.

mechanism.text: The audience reconstructs the geometry of the space from the direction each character faces. Two characters facing the same way cannot be facing each other, so the audience infers a third party rather than a mistake.

caveats.text: the source states the requirement absolutely: both shots must come from the initial side of the arc, never one from each

item.claim: Technique 8.7. For an argument, hold a wide master with almost no camera movement and let the actors circle and pace, blocked so that whoever is dominating the scene faces the camera and the turn has already happened before the other begins to dominate. The source states the standing problem — one actor is always facing away — and requires that actor to be given enough body acting to keep a presence. It also gives a fallback: if no take is perfect, shoot coverage that need not be faces, since hands and feet will enable a cut while keeping the focus on the argument's energy.

mechanism.text: People arguing circle and pace, so the movement the scene needs is already there; making the actors carry it keeps the audience oriented in a way a moving camera would not.

item.claim: The editor cannot compose the shots but chooses which compositions meet at a cut. Placing one character at frame left with open look room to the right, and cutting to a matching shot of the other character at frame right with look room to the left, makes the viewer's gaze travel across the screen at the cut and land on the new face. The source calls this eye-line match or eye trace and likens the effect to a tennis ball crossing a court.

mechanism.text: While watching character A at frame left the viewer is aware that A's attention is directed across the screen to the right. At the cut the viewer traces that eye-line across the empty look room and is rewarded by finding character B where the trace ended.

scope.conditions: two-person dialogue coverage with matching reciprocal singles

source_terms: M: They were painting essences, and in order to paint an essence you have to paint it from its most characteristic angle.
M: That's exactly what we do in film, except that instead of the body of the person, it's the work itself.
M: It may be, five hundred years from now, when people see films from our era, they'll seem "Egyptian" in a strange way.
item.claim: Murch's analogy for what shot selection is. Ancient Egyptian painters showed each part of a body from the angle that revealed most about it — face in profile, shoulders frontal, hips frontal, feet in profile — combining the characteristic essences of a person in one figure, which produces a strange twisted effect that was natural to them. Film does exactly the same, he says, except that the thing being composed is the work rather than a body: the director chooses the most characteristic, revealing, interesting angle for every situation, line and scene, overshoots, and gives the editor a further range of choices; the editor then shifts between angles on the same principle. He adds that in five hundred years films of this era may look equally strange or comic.

mechanism.text: Both practices reject reproducing a single viewpoint faithfully in favour of assembling the most revealing view of each element. What looks natural is a convention, which is why it can later look comic.

scope.conditions: any multi-angle coverage of a scene

caveats.text: the analogy carries the argument entirely; no evidence is offered that Egyptian painting and film coverage share anything beyond the described resemblance

the closing move — that our own convention may look comic in five hundred years — is the chapter's one explicit statement that current film grammar is historically contingent rather than natural. It arrives as an aside.

DISCLOSED CONTAMINATION. I recognised this analogy while reading this source because I had extracted a compressed version of the same argument from In the Blink of an Eye earlier in this lane, where it appears as a footnote. Nothing was imported: this object is written from the wording in front of me, which is substantially longer and differently developed. The recognition is disclosed here and discussed in the book 12 findings, because an extraction cannot claim independence it does not have.

and lens choice is one dimension of choosing the revealing view

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Centered-Axis Structure, caption to the paired advertisements (spine 6)
item.question: Can symmetry and asymmetry be used in the same composition, on Samara's account? State his position and its condition exactly.
item.answer: His position is that they rarely combine effectively, but that bringing the two kinds of organisational structure into confrontation can yield interesting results — on one condition, that the two compositional states remain distinct. He gives no test for how distinct is distinct enough. The condition is worth noticing because it is a rule shape that recurs through the chapter: a departure works while the state departed from is still legible as a separate state, which is also why he says a deconstructed grid should leave a recognisable vestige.
item.support: Caption in "Centered-Axis Structure": symmetry and asymmetry rarely combine effectively, but confrontation can yield interesting results so long as the two compositional states are distinct.
confounders: reading it as a straight prohibition
reading it as unconditional permission — the condition is the whole content of the claim
assuming the two states should be blended into each other, which is the opposite of what he requires

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Centered-Axis Structure (spine 6)
item.question: A centred layout for a cultural institution has been criticised as inert. Samara predicts this failure. What does he say causes it, and what are his remedies — noting which dimension the remedies are allowed to touch?
item.answer: He says symmetry is unforgiving with regard to layout flexibility because it demands that every element adhere to a single axis, and elements that do not typically appear disunified from the whole. The resulting restfulness and uniformity are problematic relative to the goals of designed communication: a viewer is likely to gloss over the material and come to an intellectual rest quickly rather than investigate the work more intently. His remedies all work on the dimensions symmetry does not govern, because moving elements off the axis is precisely what is unavailable. Exaggerate contrasts in scale or proportion and in spacing, density and rhythm. Enlarge the symmetrically organised forms until they are clearly bigger than the remaining symmetrical spaces, so their confrontation with the format becomes tense and the static quality is reduced. Juxtapose dramatically different emphases in proportion, among both the forms and the spaces between them, under a defined logic of progression or alternation along the axis. And make radical changes in size or in lightness and darkness so that lateral movement is reordered as movement from near to far.
item.support: "Centered-Axis Structure": symmetry unforgiving, elements off-axis appear disunified, viewer comes to intellectual rest quickly; exaggerating contrasts in scale and spacing as critical to optical vitality; oversized forms creating tension with the format; a logic of progression along the axis; radical size and value changes reordering movement dimensionally.
confounders: recommending that elements be moved off the axis, which is the one repair symmetry forecloses
assuming restfulness is the goal of a symmetrical layout; Samara treats it as the problem
reaching for colour variety in general — his named levers are scale, spacing/density, and lightness/darkness

item.question: What licensed spending in the household this source describes, and what was treated as the enemy?
item.answer: An occasion licensed spending; impulse was the enemy. He describes growing up in middle-class India as 'an elaborate exercise in learning to detach action from one's senses' — ice cream was not eaten because one felt like it but on occasions when celebrations had been planned, and new clothes were bought with ceremony at festivals. Festivals functioned as 'the safety valves in our otherwise restrained lives', supplying permission the individual's own appetite was not allowed to supply. The mechanism is that where budgets are tight and every deviation is felt as risk, the sense that prompts spending has to be disconnected from the act, and an external calendar then supplies the sanction.
item.support: 'Festivals were the safety valves in our otherwise restrained lives; they gave us sanction to experience little atolls of freedom.'
item.confounders: Wholly retrospective — an adult recalling a childhood household with no contemporaneous record — and the book's second section is explicitly about these constraints loosening.

source_terms: Framing the shot usually comes before anything else—the first decision.

Composition (or design if you like) covers the whole range of organizing the image, while framing concentrates on enclosing the scene, even before thinking about the relationship between elements inside the picture.
item.claim: Framing and composition are different acts. Framing concentrates on enclosing the scene and comes before anything else, prior even to thinking about relationships between the elements inside the picture; composition covers the whole range of organising the image. The source notes the term comes from filmmaking, where a scene is enclosed and the action then plays out within it, and concedes the separation is less sharp in still photography, where the image is singular rather than multiple. Even so, the decisions about where to cut into a landscape, figure or object, and what to include and leave out, rank as the most important in defining the shot.

mechanism.text: In film the enclosure is fixed first and the action happens inside it, which is what makes framing logically prior. The source imports that ordering into still photography while acknowledging it fits less cleanly.

caveats.text: the source states directly that the separation may not hold to the same degree in still photography
the claim that framing decisions are the most important in defining the shot is asserted and is not revisited or tested anywhere in the three parts

intra_source_relations.note: placing is treated as the next decision after framing

source_terms: A difference in proportion between an image and its surrounding space can create dramatic tension that will almost guarantee a dynamic composition, even if only one image appears.
item.claim: A second way to build from images is through how their shape relates to the format they appear in. A difference in proportion between an image and its surrounding space creates dramatic tension that will almost guarantee a dynamic composition even where only one image appears. The image's shape can define a module; comparing two images of the same or different proportions and finding a correspondence between them can yield a module allowing both to be shown at different scales; or the grid may simply be columns whose measure is a fractional subdivision of the image's width at the size wanted. Which route is taken depends partly on what other content accompanies the images — if the supporting content is not complex or varied, a very simple structure may be perfectly useful.

caveats.text: "almost guarantee" is the source's hedge; no test distinguishes a productive proportional difference from an awkward one

source_terms: Pacing can be understood as a kind of cadence or “timing” a viewer will apprehend from one part to another, as well as the degree of dynamism or activity they perceive.
ordering is about function; pacing is about feeling
item.claim: Rhythmic pacing from part to part within a sequence-based format is a powerful way of keeping a grid's use lively. Pacing is the cadence or timing a viewer apprehends from one part to the next, and the degree of dynamism they perceive. Varying it from slow to fast or quiet to dynamic does two things: each new page or screen engages the reader afresh, and the reader is cued to a significant change of content, which clarifies informational function. Pacing is distinct from ordering, which accounts for the location and actual sequence of raw content; pacing is the formal variation imposed on that. Ordering is about function; pacing is about feeling. Applying the system's rules for sizes, weights and styles will automatically create a recognisable rhythm supporting the informational ordering, but that intrinsic pacing may seem too even for the designer's concept, and it falls to the designer to balance deriving pacing from the content's own ordering against invigorating the viewer.

mechanism.text: A change in formal treatment is read as a change in kind, so varying the rhythm signals a content boundary without any explicit marker.

caveats.text: the source says pacing is somewhat intuitive and offers being methodical only as an initial aid — sketching an abstract or iconic storyboard of the visual states to be achieved
the source states the tension as arguable in both directions and leaves it to the designer, which is the section's most explicit refusal to decide

source_terms: Tension is not the same as fear
If you feel like you're coercing people, manipulating them or causing them to be afraid, you're probably doing it wrong
Fear's a dream killer. It puts people into suspended animation, holding their breath, paralyzed and unable to move forward
There might be fear, but tension is the promise that we can get through that fear to the other side
Tension is the hallmark of a great educational experience
item.claim: Godin draws a distinction he treats as the ethical boundary of his method. Fear paralyses: it puts people into suspended animation, holding their breath, unable to move forward, and fear alone will not produce change. Tension is different in kind — it is the promise that you can get through the fear to the other side, the state of "this might work versus this might not work", and the state of knowing you do not yet know something. He calls tension the hallmark of a great educational experience and says all effective education creates it, because just before you learn something you are aware you do not know it. His practical test for having crossed the line is subjective and he offers no other: if you feel like you are coercing, manipulating or frightening people, you are probably doing it wrong.

mechanism.text: Fear and tension are both discomfort; they differ in whether a route out is visible. Where forward motion is available the discomfort is a reason to move, and where it is not the same discomfort produces immobility.

scope.conditions: any attempt to move someone off an established behaviour

caveats.text: The test is the marketer's own feeling. Godin supplies no criterion the person on the receiving end could apply, and several of his own approved cases — the colleague saying "you're missing out", the fear of social isolation as a joining motive — sit close to the line he is drawing.

"Once we see a way out, the tension can be the tool that moves us" makes the availability of forward motion the whole distinction. Whether the route out is genuinely available, or only appears to be, is the question the framing does not ask.

source_stated_problems: coercing people, manipulating them or causing them to be afraid
Fear will paralyze us if we haven't been taught that forward motion is possible
source_stated_remedies: generously and respectfully create tension on behalf of that change

positive.description: the state of not quite knowing where you are in a curriculum, offered as the tension all effective education creates

intra_source_relations.note: names the boundary the tension mechanism must not cross
tension is the answer to the conservatism of fitting in and status
